title: How to Avoid Focusing on Irrelevant Information When Making a Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note challenges the assumption that more information always improves decisions, citing research showing that even small amounts of irrelevant information can derail quality decision-making by pulling attention toward facts that shouldn't carry weight. The remedy is deciding, before gathering any information, exactly what is relevant and what is explicitly out of bounds -- illustrated with a hiring example where factors like grades or political views shouldn't influence candidate selection but often creep in and distort discussion anyway.
points: Research shows even small amounts of irrelevant information can derail otherwise sound decision-making.
The key skill is deciding what information is relevant before collection begins, not filtering after the fact.
A hiring example illustrates how irrelevant factors like grades or political views can distort candidate evaluation.
Brainstorming the essential questions a decision needs answered is recommended as a filtering exercise.
Good decision-makers actively call out and shut down irrelevant information raised during discussions.
quotes: Leaders sometimes think putting all the facts and data on the table will clarify the problem and make an obvious decision clear. It doesn’t. It sometimes makes it worse.
Research has shown that even small amounts of irrelevant or surplus information can derail the ability to make quality decisions.
An important first step is to decide exactly what information is needed. Do this even before embarking on the process of collecting information.
The best decision-makers call out irrelevant facts and information that are raised during discussions and hold a hard line against discussing them.
When it comes to decision-making, what you don’t consider can have as much impact on a decision as what you do.
